newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-HENMAN'S BARMY ARMY SILENCED BY CHANG.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-HENMAN'S BARMY ARMY SILENCED BY CHANG.

text.p: They danced, they cheered, they sang. They were typically embarrassing Britons abroad.
But Tim Henman's "Barmy Army" soon fell silent when Michael Chang went to work and demolished Britain's grand slam dream.
Friday's third round tie at the Australian Open between fast rising Henman and American world number two Chang generated genuine interest -- and a lot of hype.
Seven months ago Henman gained national fame when he became the first British male to reach the quarter-finals of Wimbledon for more than 20 years.

A week ago the 22-year-old ousted world number three Goran Ivanisevic en route to capturing his first professional title. The nation which put lawn tennis on the map began to believe it had again produced someone who could beat the world at it.
But under the floodlights of the Melbourne Park centre court, former French Open champion Chang put "Henmania" back into the bottle with a world class performance.

Henman showed occasional brilliance as he lost 6-1 7-6 6-3, but no consistency. Chang showed both, serving as powerfully as his small frame would allow, producing deftly placed lobs when Henman pushed against the net, and chasing around the court after every ball he could.

There were times during the match when the Briton could have stemmed the tide, notably when he was serving at 5-3 in the second set having won two breaks of service against one for Chang. He lost the game without winning a point.

Henman claims to be unburdened by the hopes of British tennis-lovers forced to keep their grand slam aspirations in check since the great Fred Perry won the last of his three Wimbledons more than 60 years ago.
He did not hide his disappointment at his defeat, blaming it on his own poor performance, but nor did he want to read too much into it.
"I had a bad day at the office, I'm not going to look into it any more than that," Henman said. "I think when I walk out of that door I'll probably have forgotten about it already."

The Barmy Army -- several dozen young men and women carrying national flags and sporting English premier league soccer shirts -- were also trying to forget it as they left Melbourne Park still singing their Henman songs.
On their way out, at the stadium's main gate, they passed a signpost pointing the way to the the world's grand slam venues. Wimbledon, it said, 16,999 km.
On Friday it must have felt more like a million kilometres.
